name: Contact lens hygiene break
lead: A contact lens hygiene break refers to pausing contact lens wear and following careful lens hygiene to reduce eye redness. It appears in looksmaxxing lists as a way to get fewer red eyes.

Wikipedia's contact lens article reports that the American Academy of Ophthalmology recommends the rub-and-rinse cleaning method and replacing lens cases at least every three months, and that wearing lenses past their replacement schedule or sleeping in daily-wear lenses raises infection risk.[1] It also says that if discomfort persists, taking a day off from wear may resolve it, and that severe or lasting discomfort should be checked by an eye doctor.[1]
infobox: None found for breaks as a treatment

paras: Wikipedia summarises hygiene advice: wash hands before handling lenses, avoid water for cleaning because tap water can carry Acanthamoeba, and use the rub-and-rinse method, which the US FDA asked manufacturers in 2010 to reflect by removing no-rub labelling.[1]

Wikipedia notes that microbial keratitis is regarded as the most significant complication of lens wear, with Pseudomonas aeruginosa the most common pathogen, and that contact lens acute red eye is a group of inflammatory complications of wear.[1] Sleeping in lenses not approved for extended wear is linked to infection, ulcers and corneal neovascularization.[1]
No studies found on a planned hygiene break as a method of reducing redness for appearance.

timeline.event: US FDA asks manufacturers to remove no-rub labelling from lens solutions.[1]

card.summary: Pausing lens wear and cleaning properly is aimed at fewer red eyes; no study tests it for looks.
card.note: Persistent redness or pain warrants an eye doctor, per general guidance.

quick.overview:
This is the practice of taking time off from contact lenses and keeping them clean so the eyes look less red.

Sources describe hygiene standards and note a day without lenses can ease discomfort, but no study tests breaks for appearance.
quick.mechanism: Lens wear can cause irritation and inflammation; resting the eye and good cleaning aim to reduce it.
quick.risks: Poor hygiene and overnight wear are linked to infections and corneal problems; severe or lasting symptoms call for an eye doctor.
